title: CBT cognitive-behavioural model
content: CBT commonly examines how a situation, a person's interpretation, emotions, bodily responses and behaviour can influence one another. Formulation is individualized; this is a working model, not a claim that every difficulty is caused by thinking errors.
clinical_caution: CBT is not about blaming a person for distress. Context, lived experience, physical health, relationships and structural stressors matter.

title: Collaborative formulation
content: A CBT formulation is a shared, revisable explanation of the links among the client's difficulties, triggers, interpretations, emotions, body responses, behaviours and maintaining factors. It should be checked with the client and updated when evidence changes.
clinical_caution: Do not treat a formulation as a diagnosis or as proven fact; record uncertainty and the client's own understanding.

title: Collaborative goal setting
content: Agree on goals with the client, making them personally meaningful, specific enough to review, and sensitive to the client's context and preferences.
clinical_caution: The Copilot may help organize proposed goals but must not set clinical goals unilaterally.

title: Baseline and progress review
content: Review the problem the client wants help with, relevant context, functioning, strengths, preferences and change over time. Use suitable measures only when selected by a qualified professional and appropriate to the setting.
clinical_caution: Do not invent scores, interpret a measure outside its instructions, or substitute a summary for a professional assessment.

title: Structured session with flexibility
content: CBT is often structured and goal-oriented, with review of recent events, collaborative agenda setting, focused work, summary and planning for practice between sessions. Structure should be adapted to client needs.
clinical_caution: A template is a guide, not a rigid script; distress, accessibility needs or urgent concerns can change the session plan.

title: Automatic thoughts
content: Automatic thoughts are rapid interpretations or images that arise in a situation and may influence emotion and behaviour. A therapist can help a client notice and examine them with curiosity.
clinical_caution: Do not assume a thought is inaccurate merely because it is negative or distressing.

title: Thought record
content: A thought record can help a client note a situation, emotion, automatic thought, evidence or alternative perspectives, and any change in feeling or action. Use the format chosen by the therapist.
clinical_caution: The worksheet is a reflective aid, not an objective truth detector or a replacement for clinical judgment.

title: Socratic questioning
content: Collaborative questions can help a client examine evidence, context, alternative explanations, usefulness and what they would say to someone they care about. Questions should be respectful and non-leading.
clinical_caution: Avoid cross-examination, argument, or pressuring a client to adopt the therapist's preferred interpretation.

title: Balanced alternative perspective
content: A client may develop a more balanced perspective by considering evidence for and against an interpretation and incorporating information previously overlooked.
clinical_caution: The aim is accuracy and flexibility, not forced positivity or minimization of real harm.

title: Cognitive distortions as hypotheses
content: Terms such as all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization or catastrophizing can be used as tentative prompts for exploring a thought pattern when relevant to the client's formulation.
clinical_caution: Do not label a client's thought automatically or use labels to dismiss justified concerns.

title: Core beliefs and assumptions
content: CBT may explore deeper beliefs and conditional assumptions when relevant to the client's difficulties and formulation, while linking this work to current experiences and goals.
clinical_caution: Do not infer core beliefs from a single utterance; treat them as hypotheses to discuss collaboratively.

title: Behavioural activation
content: Behavioural activation helps identify relationships between activity, avoidance and mood, then plan manageable activities linked to values, routine, mastery or connection.
clinical_caution: Activity plans must be feasible and adapted to disability, illness, safety, resources and the client's circumstances.

title: Activity monitoring
content: Monitoring activities alongside mood, energy or context can help a client and therapist notice patterns and identify potential next steps.
clinical_caution: Monitoring should not become burdensome or increase shame; use a simpler format if needed.

title: Graded task planning
content: A large or avoided task can be broken into smaller, concrete steps and scheduled collaboratively to make it more approachable.
clinical_caution: Do not frame inability to complete a task as failure; review barriers and adapt the plan.

title: Behavioural experiment
content: A behavioural experiment is collaboratively designed to examine a specific prediction by collecting observable information in a safe, proportionate way.
clinical_caution: Experiments are not coercive exposure. Assess context and risk; use qualified clinical oversight for high-distress or specialized interventions.

title: Avoidance and maintenance cycles
content: Avoidance may reduce distress in the short term while sometimes maintaining a problem over time. Explore the function and context of the behaviour before considering change.
clinical_caution: Avoidance can be protective in unsafe contexts; never assume all avoidance should be reduced.

title: Structured problem solving
content: When a difficulty is practical and changeable, define the problem, generate options, consider likely consequences, choose a feasible next step and review what happened.
clinical_caution: Do not recast systemic, financial, medical or safety problems as merely a thinking problem.

title: Coping strategy review
content: Help the client identify coping responses that have helped, those that have costs, and possible alternatives aligned with their goals.
clinical_caution: Avoid moralizing or assuming a coping response is maladaptive without understanding its function.

title: Between-session practice
content: Practice between sessions can help a client try skills in everyday contexts and bring observations back to therapy. Agree on tasks collaboratively and review barriers without blame.
clinical_caution: Homework is not a compliance test; adapt or omit it when inappropriate or burdensome.

title: Reviewing practice barriers
content: If a practice task was not completed, explore factors such as clarity, timing, energy, accessibility, confidence, competing demands or whether the task felt useful.
clinical_caution: Do not infer lack of motivation or engagement from non-completion alone.

title: Therapeutic alliance and collaboration
content: CBT work depends on a respectful working relationship, shared understanding and collaboration. Invite feedback and acknowledge when a strategy does not fit.
clinical_caution: The AI assistant must not impersonate a therapist or imply that a human therapeutic relationship exists with the AI.

title: Adapt language and materials
content: Use plain language, accessible formats and a pace suited to the client's needs. Check understanding and preferences rather than assuming reading level or digital access.
clinical_caution: Do not infer literacy, disability, culture or language preference from demographic proxies; ask or use verified information.

title: Cultural and contextual adaptation
content: Interpret thoughts and behaviours in their social, cultural, family, work, physical-health and material context. Collaboratively adapt examples and interventions to the person.
clinical_caution: Avoid treating culturally grounded beliefs or realistic responses to discrimination as cognitive errors by default.

title: Choice of delivery format
content: CBT may be delivered in different formats, including individual, group, guided self-help or digital formats depending on the clinical problem, evidence, suitability and local service availability.
clinical_caution: Do not promise availability, eligibility or outcomes; follow local service and clinician decisions.

title: Reviewing progress and fit
content: Review progress and the fit of the formulation and intervention with the client. If improvement is limited, consider barriers, preferences, context, formulation and whether another approach or further assessment is needed.
clinical_caution: The Copilot should surface a review prompt, not independently declare treatment failure or prescribe a change.

title: Relapse-prevention planning
content: Planning may include identifying personal warning signs, triggers, helpful skills, supports and practical steps to take if difficulties return.
clinical_caution: Plans should be individualized and agreed with the client and treating professional; do not guarantee prevention.

title: CBT is not a universal solution
content: CBT is one of several psychological approaches. Suitability depends on the person's needs, preferences, circumstances, presenting problem and available qualified care.
clinical_caution: Do not recommend CBT as the only or automatically best option for every person.

title: Professional assessment and treatment decisions
content: Treatment selection, diagnosis, risk assessment and changes to care require appropriate qualified professionals and the relevant service pathway.
clinical_caution: The Copilot can summarize evidence and suggest questions for a clinician; it must not diagnose, prescribe, change medication or replace professional assessment.

title: Urgent risk or crisis disclosure
content: If a client discloses imminent danger, suicidal intent, abuse or another urgent safety concern, the system should follow the organization's approved escalation and safeguarding protocol and direct the issue to a qualified human.
clinical_caution: Do not rely on a CBT worksheet or generic coping exercise as a substitute for crisis assessment. Do not invent emergency pathways; configure local protocol.

title: Physical symptoms need appropriate assessment
content: CBT may address interpretations and coping related to physical sensations in relevant formulations, but physical symptoms may also require medical assessment.
clinical_caution: Never dismiss new, severe or unexplained symptoms as anxiety or a cognitive distortion; follow clinical protocols.

title: No forced positive reframing
content: Balanced thinking means considering the available evidence and context, including genuine risks and injustice. It does not require optimism or denial of painful events.
clinical_caution: Do not pressure a client to minimize trauma, discrimination, grief or material hardship.

title: Concise session summary
content: A session summary can capture the client's stated focus, collaboratively identified links, skills discussed, client response, agreed practice and unresolved questions.
clinical_caution: Distinguish client-reported information, therapist observation, model inference and unknowns. Do not fabricate events or outcomes.

content: When the Copilot uses CBT knowledge, keep source identifiers and retrieval provenance available so a professional can inspect the basis for a suggestion.

title: Use evidence with context
content: Clinical guidance may describe recommended interventions for particular populations and severity levels; apply recommendations within their stated scope and consider updates and local pathways.

title: Thought-emotion-behaviour links are individual
content: Explore how a particular interpretation relates to a client's emotion, body response and behaviour in a particular situation; the same event can be experienced differently by different people.
clinical_caution: Do not assume a universal or deterministic link between one thought and one emotion or behaviour.

title: Small, observable next step
content: When appropriate, collaboratively identify a small, observable action that supports a client-defined goal and decide how the client will review what they learn.
